/comparison.text: comparison the audio is the difference. polyemesis is built for one case, completely: this platform gets the clean mix, that one gets the full mix, from a single upload and a single video encode, with the picture never re-encoded to do it. that is the case the whole product is arranged around: the routing matrix, the per-destination loudness targets, the multitrack archive and the stems all exist because the audio is the hard part, and because everywhere else it is a track you pick rather than a mix you build. the short version if you do not need different audio per platform, restreamer is a more mature product and you should probably use it. multistreaming from the stream pc: obs-multi-rtmp is free, mature and enough. a server instead: restreamer is more mature and far more widely deployed than this. no server at all: restream.io. an industrial-strength media server with real track selection: mistserver. polyemesis exists for the one case none of them serve. if that is not your problem, one of the tools above is the better fit. compared one at a time if you already run something, start here. each page compares polyemesis against one of them in full, with that tool's strengths stated and every claim dated against its own sources. aitum multistream obs plugin · free · gpl-2.0 it already sends different audio per platform. the argument is about where the mix gets built, and what a third one costs. read the comparison obs-multi-rtmp obs plugin · free · gpl-2.0 get from obs means fanning out costs one encode, not four. what it cannot share is your uplink: the same bytes, sent once per platform. read the comparison restreamer and restream.io server · saas · two different products two unrelated things share the name. neither can build a second mix at all, and one of them bills per channel. read the comparison streamelements obs plugin · free · windows only the dashboard everyone knows sends no video at all. the multistreaming is se.live, which is windows-only and speaks no srt. read the comparison streamlabs cloud relay · ultra subscription their servers do the fan-out, and multistreaming proper is behind the paid tier. the free path stops at two destinations. read the comparison twitch multistreaming is the case most of these are bought for, and all five do it. the tables below are what separates them once that is assumed. where they differ one axis, and it is the one this project exists for. the shared ground (everything all three do) is in the table below this one. capability polyemesis restreamer restream.io per-destination audio mix from one multitrack ingest yes no no channel-level mix matrix with per-cell gain yes no no per-destination loudness target you set - i, lra and tp, measured after routing yes multitrack archive - every ingest track preserved, stream-copied yes not assessed not assessed per-track stems as 24-bit wav or flac, segment-aligned yes not assessed not assessed track annotations - what each incoming track actually is yes not assessed not assessed typed srt rejections - the publisher is told why it was refused yes not assessed not assessed a second audio mix to the same destination, from one ingest yes: twitch enhanced broadcasting, needs a gpu - - runs on hardware you control, no per-destination pricing yes yes no experimental on the second-audio-mix row, and only where the destination is twitch. the negotiation itself is proven: polyemesis's tests reach ingest.twitch.tv on every run, and twitch accepts a supported-gpu inventory, grants the vod audio track and mints a key. what nobody has watched yet is a broadcast published through that key. off twitch the two-mix egress is a different mechanism and is not covered by this. nothing is gated either way: a negotiation that does not succeed falls back to the ordinary twitch ingest. the multitrack ask is not hypothetical. "multiple audio tracks for twitch" was an open request on restreamer's own tracker when this was surveyed in july 2026: users asking it for the thing polyemesis was built to be. choose another tool when each of these is a job another tool is built for. they are worth reading before you spend an evening on an install: they follow from design decisions and the project's age, not from a roadmap, so the right tool for these jobs today is the one named. choose the obs plugins for obs-multi-rtmp and aitum multistream: free, gpl-2.0, installed in two minutes and already on the machine. no server at all a plugin in obs: no host to provision, no port to open. here you run a server, or there is nothing to run. nothing new to learn the destinations sit in obs beside the ones already there. here it is a second ui and a second set of concepts. no extra hop obs talks to the platform directly, so nothing in the middle can fail. here the server is one more thing between you and air. per-target video encoder settings, decided in obs here that is a shared rendition, decided on the server. what they cost you is upload: n destinations is n uploads off one connection, and n video encodes on the machine also running the show. if your upload is comfortable, that is not a reason to put a server in the path. choose restreamer for ranked by how often each was asked for on their own tracker, which is the honest ordering. webrtc / whip output not in polyemesis. a sizeable subsystem; the real use case is sub-second self-monitoring. decklink / sdi capture, in and out not in polyemesis. it needs an ffmpeg built with decklink, so a third image variant. multi-input compositing / video grid not in polyemesis. natural once multi-source is settled. hdr 10-bit hevc partial in polyemesis. libx265 and hevc_nvenc exist; there is no hdr tone-map path. ll-hls declined in polyemesis, not built. ffmpeg cannot emit ll-hls partial segments at all, so the protocol would need a go-side packager. tuning instead took preview latency from 4.2-6.2 s to 2.2-3.2 s, measured. maturity choose mistserver for the one tool here that is a peer rather than a different shape, at a scale and protocol breadth this project does not approach. protocol breadth a directory of muxers, including webrtc and its own srt output. here: srt, srtla and rtmp in, rtmp/srt out, hls for preview. years of production deployment, and a commercial vendor behind it selection without decoding a push target that only selects tracks is a pure copy end to end. every polyemesis destination decodes and re-encodes its audio, always, because that is what mixing is. choose restream.io for saas. self-hosting wins on cost, privacy and limits by construction; restream.io wins wherever having somebody else run it is the feature. studio: browser production, remote guests not in polyemesis. multi-source plus compositing is the closest path. teams, roles, multiple workspaces not in polyemesis, which has exactly one admin identity. no server to run polyemesis is self-hosted by design. teams and roles is the one to take seriously. access to the ui is full control of the server's streaming, so any multi-operator deployment (a church a/v team, an agency running several clients) hits that immediately. these come from docs/comparison.md , which carries the same rows with their evidence, their issue numbers and the date each was checked, including the footnotes recording the rows that were wrong and were corrected, in both directions: some had gone stale understating this product, and twice a cell asserted a competitor lacked something they ship. they select a track. polyemesis mixes. most people weighing this up already have one of these installed. the distinction against every one of them is the same narrow one, and it is narrow enough to be worth checking rather than believing: they decide which track leaves for a destination. none of them decides what is in it. obs-multi-rtmp an obs plugin. each destination is another output from the stream pc, so n destinations is n uploads off one connection. struct audiotrackconfig { int mixer_track; int output_track; }; src/output-config.h · read 2026-08-09 two integers: this mixer track goes in that output slot. no gain, no sum. full comparison against obs-multi-rtmp aitum multistream an obs plugin. the destination's audio is picked in its output settings and stored as one number. obs_audio_encoder_create(…, obs_data_get_int(settings, "audio_track"), …) multistream.cpp · read 2026-08-09 one mixer index per destination. full comparison against aitum multistream mistserver a media server, and the one here that genuinely can pick tracks per push target: by track id, codec, language, bitrate, or a first/last/optimal heuristic. competitor-facts §6 · checked 15 aug 2026 it selects, and selects well. its routing server has no amix, no loudnorm, no ebur128, but an external stream process (mistprocav, an ffmpeg pipeline) can decode, filter and inject a track back into the buffer, so mixing is reachable, just not where the routing happens. polyemesis sums instead: the tracks you chose, with a gain per input-channel-to-output-channel cell, and a loudness target measured after the routing rather than before it. that is a different operation, which is why per-destination audio is not a small patch to an obs plugin. it costs something, and the cost belongs on this page too. selecting a track is a copy; mixing means decoding the audio and encoding it again on every destination. only the video is copied straight through. if one mix for everyone is fine, a plugin is free and you should use one. what all three do the basic job is table stakes everywhere: ingest once, fan out, reconnect when a platform drops, show you whether it is working. worth stating plainly: it means the choice between these three comes down to the audio, and not to whether the fundamentals are there. polyemesis restreamer restream.io ingest once, fan out to several platforms yes yes yes reconnects when a platform drops yes not assessed not assessed live health and status you can watch yes not assessed not assessed recording multitrack, stream-copied no built-in not assessed metrics / api prometheus + rest not assessed not assessed hardware encoding nvenc, qsv, va-api, videotoolbox, amf yes n/a unified chat yes not assessed not assessed self-hosted yes yes no simultaneous destinations no configured cap not assessed 2-5 by plan (checked 15 aug 2026) cost your hardware your hardware subscription two rows are not a tie and are left that way: restream.io needs no server from you at all, and restreamer has a far longer public release history. both are real advantages, and neither changes what happens to your audio. experimental on the hardware-encoding row: all five encoders are offered, and each is probed with a real one-frame encode at startup so one that is listed but unusable is caught before a broadcast is. what is unverified is narrower: the command-line flags handed to nvenc, qsv, va-api and amf were read out of ffmpeg's own option tables rather than measured on silicon. videotoolbox is not in that set: a real encode with its own flags runs on every build. the recording row said "yes" for restreamer until 9 august 2026 and was wrong. recording is an open request on their own tracker , opened february 2024 and still open when it was checked. the datarhei core underneath can write files; the restreamer product does not put recording in front of you, which is why the request exists. rows and cards carry their own check date where one exists. the oldest reads here are from july 2026, re-checked 9 august 2026; the mistserver, streamelements and streamlabs material was read 15-16 august 2026. these products move independently of this page, so check them before deciding on the strength of a row. still the right problem? then the next thing to read is the one that tells you what running it is actually like, and that is the quickstart rather than the download page. read the quickstart this page, with its sources try the routing matrix · install options

/vs/aitum-multistream.h1: Aitum Multistream picks a mix. polyemesis builds one.
h2: The same broadcast, set up both ways
/vs/aitum-multistream.text: polyemesis / comparison / aitum multistream compared aitum multistream picks a mix. polyemesis builds one. the aitum multistream obs plugin can already send different audio to different platforms; anyone telling you otherwise has not used it. each destination is assigned one of obs's six audio tracks, and that track goes out. the question this page answers is a narrower one: where the mix on that track gets made, and what it costs you to have more than one. the difference in one sentence: aitum selects a mix obs has already built, so three different mixes means three track layouts maintained in advanced audio properties and each output encoded on the stream pc. polyemesis sums the tracks server-side, so one upload and one video encode feed every destination. the same broadcast, set up both ways two destinations. twitch takes the music, youtube does not. both tools finish this job, and comparing the routes is more useful than comparing a column of yes against a column of no. in obs, with aitum multistream every step is on the stream pc. 1 open advanced audio properties and build the layout: mic and game on track 1, mic and game and music on track 2. this is the mix, and this is where it is made. 2 add the twitch destination in aitum, set its audio track to 2. 3 add the youtube destination, set its audio track to 1. 4 choose an encoder for each destination, or clone the main obs output for both. 5 both destinations now upload from this machine. in polyemesis one upload leaves the stream pc. the rest happens on the server. 1 in obs, put each source on its own track: mic on 1, game on 2, music on 3. no layout to design, because nothing is being summed yet. 2 send one multitrack srt stream to polyemesis. 3 tick the tracks each destination should hear: twitch gets 1, 2 and 3; youtube gets 1 and 2. 4 change your mind mid-broadcast by unticking a box. the track layout in obs never moves. at two destinations these are the same amount of work, and the honest summary is that it does not matter which you pick. the divergence starts at the third: a new mix in aitum is a new track layout in obs, and obs has six tracks. in polyemesis a new mix is a row of checkboxes, and the thing being ticked is the ingest, which has not changed. where the work lands not a capability difference. a location difference, and on a machine that is also running the game, location is the whole argument. aitum multistream the mixing desk is obs's advanced audio properties. the encoders run on the stream pc, one per destination unless you clone the main output. every destination uploads from your connection. polyemesis the mixing desk is the server, with a gain per input-channel-to-output-channel cell and a loudness target measured after the routing. one upload leaves the stream pc; the picture is copied through rather than re-encoded. the cost belongs here too, because it is real: mixing means decoding the audio and encoding it again for every destination, where selecting a track is a copy. polyemesis also needs a server, and aitum does not. if the mixes you want are ones obs can already build on its six tracks, the plugin is free and you should use it. what aitum multistream does well checked against aitum's own repository and site on 15 august 2026 . free, and gpl-2.0 the multistream plugin costs nothing. aitum sells a separate desktop automation suite, nexus, at $5.49/mo, and multistream does not require it. per-destination encoding each destination can clone the main obs output or re-encode independently, with its own resolution, bitrate and encoder. that is not a lesser feature than what a server does. it is the same feature, paid for locally. it is where you already are it runs inside obs. there is no server to provision, no second machine, no ingest to point anywhere. for a great many broadcasts that is the correct architecture and this page is not an argument against it. streamsuite multistream is now bundled with aitum vertical under the streamsuite name, with unified multi-chat and metadata panels alongside it. use aitum, not this one mix suits every platform. this is most broadcasts, and adding a server to serve it is a worse setup, not a better one. your track layout is settled and you are not editing it under load. you want a destination at a different resolution or bitrate and your pc has the headroom to encode it. aitum does this natively. you do not want to run, patch or pay for a server. that is a legitimate position and there is no answer to it here. polyemesis is worth the server when the mixes outnumber the tracks, when the stream pc has no headroom left to encode with, or when the upload is the ceiling: one stream out instead of one per platform. weighing up the others too? and is recorded in docs/evidence/competitor-facts-2026-08-15.md . prices and plan limits move; check before deciding on the strength of a number here.

h2: What actually leaves the stream PC
/vs/obs-multi-rtmp.text: polyemesis / comparison / obs-multi-rtmp compared obs-multi-rtmp uploads once per platform. the obs-multi-rtmp plugin adds a second, third and fourth rtmp output inside obs, and each one is a separate upload from the machine you are broadcasting on. that is the whole shape of it, and for most people it is fine. this page is about the point where it stops being fine, which is your connection rather than your processor. give the plugin its due first: its get from obs option shares one encoder across every destination, so multi-rtmp in obs does not cost you an encode per platform. the processor argument against it is mostly wrong. what it cannot share is the uplink: four destinations is the same bytes sent four times. what actually leaves the stream pc the plugin runs inside obs, so every destination it adds is another output from that machine. polyemesis is a server, so the machine sends one stream and the fan-out happens somewhere with a better connection than a house. what leaves the stream pc obs-multi-rtmp polyemesis video encodes running on the stream pc one, shared, with get from obs, or one per destination when you want different bitrates one, to produce the srt ingest, and still one at ten destinations. the server stream-copies the picture through untouched outbound streams from your connection one per destination one, to the server, regardless of how many destinations there are audio encodes on the stream pc one per destination one aac encode per track you send, and that count is fixed by your track layout, not by the destination list. the summing and the per-destination encode happen on the server where a mix gets summed obs's own audio mixer, upstream of the plugin the server, per destination, with a gain per channel-to-channel cell read the second row on a domestic upload. a 6 mbps broadcast to four platforms is 24 mbps sustained out of a connection that is also carrying the game, and every platform is receiving an identical copy. moving the fan-out onto a server replaces that with a single 6 mbps send, which is the argument for a server, and it is a bandwidth argument, not an audio one. it cuts the other way too, and belongs on the page: the server has to live somewhere, be patched, and be paid for. obs-multi-rtmp has no such bill and never goes down separately from obs. on the audio, precisely what it does each output is assigned one of obs's audio tracks (mixer ids 1 through 6), and that track is what the destination receives. so different platforms genuinely can get different audio, and any comparison telling you otherwise is wrong about this plugin. where the mix came from the plugin does not sum anything. tracks 1 to 6 were summed by obs's own mixer before the plugin saw them, so what you are choosing per destination is which of six pre-built mixes to send. polyemesis builds the mix per destination instead, from the tracks as they arrived. six tracks is a real ceiling and also a generous one: most broadcasts need two. the distinction earns a page because of what it costs to change: a new mix in obs is a new track layout, and it is not something to be editing while live. what obs-multi-rtmp does well checked against the project's own repository and releases on 15 august 2026 . actively maintained developed by sorayuki, at v0.7.4.3 when this was checked, with regular compatibility releases tracking obs studio 30.x, 31.x and 32.x. in a plugin ecosystem where the usual failure is silent abandonment two obs majors ago, that is the feature that matters most. get from obs is genuinely good engineering sharing the main obs encoder across every destination means fanning out to four platforms costs one encode, not four. this is the same idea as a shared rendition on a server, implemented locally, and it is the reason the cpu argument against this plugin is mostly wrong. independent re-encoding when you want it separate encoder instances per destination, with their own bitrates and resolutions, for the platform that will not take your source. free, gpl-2.0, and inside obs already no cost, no account, no server, no second machine. it ingests whatever obs ingests and publishes over rtmp and rtmps. use the plugin, not this your upload comfortably carries every destination at once. if it does, the main reason to move the fan-out off your machine has already been answered. the per-destination mixes you want are ones you can lay out across obs's six tracks. selecting one of those per output is exactly what this plugin does, at zero cost. you want no infrastructure. a plugin that ships with your broadcast software is one fewer thing to keep alive. you are already running it and it works. there is no upgrade being sold here. still weighing it up? 2026 , and is recorded in docs/evidence/competitor-facts-2026-08-15.md . prices and plan limits move; check before deciding on the strength of a number here.

/vs/restreamer.h1: Two products are called Restream. Neither gives a platform its own mix.
h2: Neither can build a second mix
The reason is upstream, at the ingest
/vs/restreamer.text: polyemesis / comparison / restreamer and restream.io compared two products are called restream. neither gives a platform its own mix. almost everyone searching for a restream alternative means one of two unrelated things, and the answers are not the same. a restreamer alternative is a replacement for datarhei's free, self-hosted, apache-2.0 server. a restream.io alternative is a replacement for a subscription. this page separates them, then makes the one argument that applies to both. which one did you mean? datarhei restreamer github.com/datarhei/restreamer a complete self-hosted restreaming server you run yourself. ingests srt, rtmp, rtmps, rtsp and hls, and publishes to as many destinations as your hardware carries. kind self-hosted server, docker licence apache-2.0 price free restream.io restream.io a cloud service that takes one stream and replicates it to your platforms, with a browser studio on top. nothing to run, and a per-channel bill. kind hosted service, subscription licence proprietary price free tier, then $19/mo neither can build a second mix this is the sharpest version of the argument on this site, and it is worth being exact about why. the obs plugins people also weigh up, obs-multi-rtmp and aitum multistream , genuinely do send different audio to different platforms, by selecting a track obs mixed for them. neither restreamer nor restream.io can do even that. restreamer per egress target the web ui offers three choices: copy the primary stream's audio, transcode the codec (aac or mp3), or force silence. there is no matrix for summing discrete channels into a new stereo mix. re-routing multiple tracks is possible, but only by writing ffmpeg pipelines by hand against the underlying rest api, which is a different product than the one the ui presents. restream.io it cannot sum tracks and it cannot select between them. the single stereo track you send is duplicated identically to every enabled endpoint. there is no per-destination audio setting because there is no second piece of audio for one to choose from. polyemesis takes a multitrack ingest and sums a mix per destination, with a gain on each input-channel-to-output-channel cell and a loudness target measured after the routing rather than before it. the clean feed goes to one platform, the full mix to the next, from one upload, and the picture is copied through rather than re-encoded to do it. the reason is upstream, at the ingest neither product is missing a mixer by oversight. neither can route a multitrack input in the first place, so there is nothing for a mixer to work on. restreamer ingests srt, rtmp, rtmps, rtsp and hls. srt arrives with a single audio track in the ui, and multitrack srt is neither exposed nor routable there. restream.io accepts rtmp, rtmps and srt. multitrack srt is not supported at all: a single stereo stream is the input contract. polyemesis takes the split audio tracks obs already knows how to send over multitrack srt and keeps them separate all the way to the point where a destination asks for a mix. what each one costs every figure below was read from the vendor's own pricing page on 15 august 2026 . tiers move. check before deciding on the strength of a number here. pricing for restreamer, restream.io and polyemesis, checked on 15 august 2026 plan price checked 15 august 2026 destinations what is included restreamer (datarhei) free, apache-2.0, self-hosted - no per-destination charge restream.io free $0 2 channels personal profiles only. no custom rtmp, no facebook pages or groups. studio capped at 720p and watermarked restream.io standard $19/mo, or $16/mo billed annually at $190/yr 3 channels no watermark. custom rtmp destinations enabled restream.io professional $49/mo, or $39/mo billed annually at $470/yr 5 channels 1080p studio. dual format: horizontal and vertical output together polyemesis free, mit, self-hosted no configured cap your hardware and your bandwidth are the bill the free-tier exclusion worth knowing before you sign up: restream.io's free plan does not include custom rtmp destinations, which is the setting anyone sending to a self-hosted or niche endpoint needs. what they do well restreamer is free, apache-2.0 and complete not a trial or an open core. it ships as a docker container, ingests over five protocols, and does per-destination re-encoding in software or hardware when a platform will not take your source. restreamer shares one ingest across destinations several destination processes pull from the single ingested internal stream without re-encoding it: the same shared-rendition idea polyemesis uses, and it has had it longer. restream.io needs no server from you that is a real advantage and no self-hosted tool answers it. there is nothing to provision, patch, monitor or pay a host for, and the fan-out runs on a connection far better than yours. restream.io keeps shipping in the twelve months to 15 august 2026 it added dual-format streaming (separate horizontal and vertical outputs at once) and automated ai clip generation. restreamer's stable line was at v2.12.0 when this was checked, with ongoing dependency and container maintenance. if one mix to every platform is what you need, it does that job for nothing and has done for years, and it is the tool this project would point you at. different audio per platform? that is the one thing neither of them does, and the reason this project exists. install polyemesis all five compared also compared: aitum multistream · obs-multi-rtmp · streamelements · streamlabs

/vs/streamelements.h1: StreamElements multistreaming is SE.Live. It runs on Windows only.
h2: Two limits worth checking before anything else
On the audio, it is the same story as the other two plugins
/vs/streamelements.text: polyemesis / comparison / streamelements compared streamelements multistreaming is se.live. it runs on windows only. anyone looking into streamelements multistream support meets a fork in the road immediately, and it is not signposted well: the streamelements almost everybody knows (overlays, tips, the chat dashboard) sends no video anywhere. the multistreaming lives in a separate obs plugin called se.live, and before comparing anything it is worth knowing which one you are holding. two facts settle most of this page: se.live is supported on windows and not on macos or linux, and it publishes over rtmp and rtmps with no srt support of any kind. the first rules it out for a lot of people outright. the second means the multitrack workflow polyemesis is built around cannot begin. which streamelements do you have? one company, two products, and only one of them touches video. streamelements cloud no video multistreaming the web dashboard. unified multi-platform chat, activity feeds, overlays and tipping. if this is the streamelements you use, it does not restream video anywhere, and nothing on this page is a comparison with it. se.live this is the multistreaming one formerly obs.live. a plugin that installs into obs studio on your own machine. everything below is about this. it is free, and it is the only video multistreaming streamelements ships. two limits worth checking before anything else neither is a matter of degree, which is why they come first. checked against streamelements' own documentation on 15 august 2026 . operating system windows, and only windows. macos and linux are not supported. nothing else compared on this site has a stop like this: the other plugins follow obs wherever it runs, and the servers are containers. if you broadcast from a mac, the comparison ends at this paragraph. transport rtmp and rtmps out. no srt, and no ingest of any kind: it captures from the obs it lives inside and is not a relay. this is the cleanest version of the difference on any of these pages. polyemesis works by receiving your separated audio tracks over multitrack srt and deciding what each platform hears from them. se.live has no way to send that, so the question of what to do with those tracks never arises. on the audio, it is the same story as the other two plugins se.live routes one obs audio track (any of the six) to each platform output. so yes, it can give twitch and youtube different sound, and a comparison claiming otherwise would be wrong. what it cannot do is combine tracks into a new mix at the output; whatever those six tracks contain was decided earlier, in obs's advanced audio properties. that is precisely the model obs-multi-rtmp and aitum multistream use, and it is argued at length on both of their pages rather than repeated here. the same argument, in full: aitum multistream · obs-multi-rtmp what se.live does well checked against streamelements' own documentation and site on 15 august 2026 . no cap on destinations, and no paid tier free at $0 with no paywall above it, and no ceiling on how many platforms you publish to: the limit is your encoding capacity and your upstream bandwidth, which is an honest limit rather than a billing one. canvas does vertical and horizontal at once its canvas system produces simultaneous 16:9 and 9:16 output from a single obs session, with twitch dual-output beta wired in. polyemesis reaches a vertical output differently: a 9:16 rendition, encoded once and shared, that crops, letterboxes or blur-fills the frame you already sent. what it cannot do is lay out a separate vertical scene; if the vertical cut needs its own composition, that is a reason to run se.live. per-destination encoding, with aspect ratio in the mix shared copy or an independent re-encode per platform, each with its own resolution, aspect, bitrate, framerate and encoder. those re-encodes run concurrently on the local machine. gpl-2.0 core, actively supported the core plugin is gpl-2.0 and openly published; the cloud backend it connects to is proprietary. nothing about it was deprecated in the year to this check. use se.live, not this you broadcast from windows and one of the six obs tracks already carries the right sound for each platform. you want the vertical cut composed as its own scene rather than reframed from the horizontal one. canvas does that in a single obs session; a polyemesis rendition can only crop, letterbox or blur-fill the frame it received. you are already inside the streamelements ecosystem for overlays, tips and chat, and adding a separate server to the setup buys you nothing you asked for. you are on windows and do not want to run a server. se.live needs no host, no port and no certificate; polyemesis needs all three before it sends a byte. polyemesis is the answer to a narrower question: you are not on windows, or you want a mix assembled per platform rather than chosen from what obs prepared, or you want the fan-out to leave a server instead of your own connection. weighing up the others too? all five compared install polyemesis also compared: streamlabs · restreamer and restream.io everything this page /vs/streamlabs.h1: Streamlabs multistreams from their servers. polyemesis multistreams from yours.
/vs/streamlabs.text: polyemesis / comparison / streamlabs compared streamlabs multistreams from their servers. polyemesis multistreams from yours. both send one upload to several platforms. the difference is whose hardware does the fan-out, whether it costs a subscription, and what each destination is allowed to hear. checked against streamlabs' own documentation on 16 august 2026. which streamlabs are you using? streamlabs ships two ways to reach more than one platform, and they are not the same product decision. multistream the cloud fan-out. twitch, youtube, tiktok, kick, facebook, patreon, x and custom rtmp. paid: an ultra feature your stream goes to streamlabs and their servers relay it onward. usable from streamlabs desktop, the streamlabs plugin for obs, or any encoder via an rtmp url from their dashboard. dual output two canvases (one vertical, one horizontal) in streamlabs desktop. free, and capped at two their words: "stream to one platform per canvas, completely free." it is the free multistreaming path, and its ceiling is two destinations of prescribed shapes rather than a number you choose. the four differences that matter their servers, or yours "we process your stream on our servers so you can expand your reach without straining your pc." that is the design, stated on their own page, and for most people it is the right trade: one upload, no hardware. polyemesis makes the opposite trade: the relay is a binary on a box you own, so nothing leaves your network except the streams you are publishing. a subscription, or not multistream proper is an ultra feature. the free tier is dual output and stops at two destinations. polyemesis is mit and has no paid tier and no cap on destinations: the limit is your upstream bandwidth and roughly 4% of one cpu core per destination, which is a physical limit rather than a billing one. rtmp in, or multitrack srt in streamlabs takes an rtmp stream, from their desktop app, their obs plugin, or any encoder pointed at their dashboard url. polyemesis ingests srt carrying up to 32 audio tracks on one connection, with rtmp as a single-track fallback. the multitrack ingest is what the per-destination mixing is built on; without it there is nothing to mix from. where the audio decision happens polyemesis sums tracks server-side and gives every destination its own stereo mix: the full mix to one platform, a music-free mix to another, a mic-only feed to a third, from one upload and one video encode. streamlabs' page does not describe per-destination audio either way, so nothing is claimed about it here; if that is the thing you need, it is a question worth putting to them directly. use streamlabs, not this if you want multistreaming without running a server, streamlabs is the easier answer and this project is not competing for that. their relay costs you one upload and no hardware, their desktop app and obs plugin are built for the job, and multichat reads and posts across youtube, twitch and facebook pages from one place. if one mix suits every platform you send to, you are already done. polyemesis is for the case where that is the thing that does not work: where the archive needs a different mix from the broadcast, where the stream must not pass through a third party, or where a subscription per month for a fan-out you could run yourself is the wrong shape. the three ways to multistream the full comparison how the mix works everything this page says about streamlabs was checked on 16 august 2026 , and is recorded in docs/evidence/competitor-facts-2026-08-15.md . prices and plan limits move; check before deciding on the strength of a number here.

/multistream.h1: Multistreaming is one upload reaching several platforms. The question is what each one hears.
/multistream.text: polyemesis / multistream multistreaming multistreaming is one upload reaching several platforms. the question is what each one hears. going live to twitch and youtube at once is a solved problem with three well-known answers. sending them different audio (the full mix to one, a music-free mix to another, your mic alone to a third) is where the three answers stop agreeing. this page covers both. the three architectures every multistreaming tool is one of these. which one you want follows from what you are short of: upload bandwidth, cpu, money, or trust in a third party. your pc does the work your streaming pc uploads a separate copy of the stream for every destination. the encode can be shared across all of them or run independently per destination. costs you upload multiplies by the number of destinations. cpu multiplies only if you re-encode per destination instead of sharing the encode obs already made. audio whatever mix that output was given. examples obs-multi-rtmp, aitum multistream, se.live: plugins that live inside obs. how the plugins compare a cloud relay you send one stream to somebody else's server. they fan it out to the platforms for you. costs you one upload. a subscription once you pass a free tier's limits, and your stream passes through a third party. audio restream.io duplicates the one stream it ingests to every endpoint, and castr sends identical audio to all destinations (both checked 2026-08-15). streamlabs does not describe per-destination audio either way, so nothing is claimed here. examples restream.io, castr, streamlabs multistream. how the cloud relays compare a relay you run you send one stream to a server you own. it fans out, on your hardware, on your network. costs you one upload. no subscription. a box to run it on. audio this is where polyemesis differs: a different mix per destination, summed server-side. examples polyemesis, datarhei restreamer, mistserver. how the self-hosted relays compare where polyemesis sits it is the third kind: a relay on hardware you control. what it adds to that category is the audio. one srt ingest carries up to 32 tracks, and each destination gets its own stereo mix summed from the tracks you choose, server-side, so your encoder uploads once and encodes video once. video is copied through untouched. that is the whole argument, and it is worth being plain about when it does not matter: if one mix suits every platform you send to, a free obs plugin does the job and you should use one. multistream from obs, three ways how the mix matrix works the full comparison a free restream service you run yourself install it per platform multistreaming to twitch twitch is the destination that makes the audio question concrete. its enhanced broadcasting can carry a second audio track alongside the live one, which is how the broadcast keeps a music bed while the archive gets a mix without it, from one upload and one encode. it needs a gpu on the machine polyemesis runs on: twitch refuses the negotiation outright when the request reports none, which matters on the vps this audience often uses. the twitch vod track, in detail multistreaming to youtube youtube takes one stereo pair, like every other live platform. multistreaming to it is unremarkable. the interesting decision is which mix it gets, and that is the same decision for every destination in the fan-out. a second audio track is not offered here. nothing in this project has measured youtube accepting one, and the code refuses to try. how a mix is chosen multistreaming to kick kick is an rtmp destination and behaves like one. polyemesis signs in to it for chat and metadata as well, so a kick fan-out is not only video: the moderation timeline reads it alongside the others. chat moderation covers five platforms: youtube, twitch, kick, facebook and rumble. facebook is read-and-moderate only; it is not in the send fan-out. what each platform can automate

/free-restream-service.text: free restream service a free restream service, if you are willing to run the server. restream does have a free tier, and it allows two simultaneous channels. if that is the answer you came for, it is at the top of the page on purpose. the rest of this is the other answer: polyemesis is a restreaming server that is free in the plain sense (mit licensed, no account, no hosted tier, nothing phoning home) because it runs on a machine you already pay for. that machine is the price, and this page is mostly about what it costs. install it what it costs you the word what a restream service actually is you send one stream out of your encoder. something downstream copies it and delivers a copy to every platform you named (twitch, youtube, kick, facebook, rumble), so your uplink carries one broadcast instead of five. that is the whole job, and every product in this category does it. the word also does double duty as a brand. restream, at restream.io, is a proprietary hosted service that does this in their cloud on a monthly subscription. if you searched for a free restream service you are probably weighing one against the other, so both are on this page: what their free tier gives you, and what running the fan-out yourself gives you instead. where products in this category diverge is not the copying. it is what happens to the audio on the way, and whether the fan-out runs on somebody else's hardware or on yours. the direct answer is restream free? checked 2026-08-15 partly. there is a free plan and it allows two simultaneous channels, to personal profiles and platforms. what it does not include is the part most people find out later: custom rtmp destinations are excluded, so a platform restream has no built-in integration for is not reachable on it, and facebook pages and groups are excluded as well. anything you produce in their browser studio carries a restream watermark and is capped at 720p. prices move. these were read off restream.io's published pricing on 2026-08-15; if that stamp is old by the time you are reading it, go and look before you rely on any of it. restream.io plans, checked 2026-08-15 plan price channels what that includes free $0 2 simultaneous channels personal profiles and platforms only. excludes custom rtmp destinations, and excludes facebook pages and groups. restream watermark on studio output, capped at 720p. standard $19/mo 3 channels $16/mo billed annually, at $190/yr. no watermark, and custom rtmp destinations are enabled. professional $49/mo 5 channels $39/mo billed annually, at $470/yr. 1080p studio, and dual-format output: horizontal and vertical at once. every figure above is recorded with its source in this repository rather than paraphrased from a competitor's marketing, and it is dated because a stale price is not a stale docs line: it is a false statement about another company's prices. if one of these has moved, that is a bug in this page and we would like to be told. the other kind of free no plan, because there is nothing to bill for. polyemesis is mit licensed and ships as one static binary or one container. there is no account to create, no free tier to graduate out of, and no telemetry. it can publish its own state over mqtt, but that is off by default and goes to a broker you name. the only runtime dependency is ffmpeg, and the container bundles it. docker copy docker run -d --name polyemesis \ -p 8080:8080 -p 6000:6000/udp -p 1935:1935 \ -v polyemesis-data:/data \ rainmanjam/polyemesis:latest note the /udp on port 6000. srt is udp, and omitting the suffix is the classic reason an ingest silently receives nothing. 1935 is published up front because a container's port mappings are fixed when it is created, so an rtmp source added later has nothing listening for it, and says so nowhere. destinations no configured cap. there is no limit in the software, but upload bandwidth and cpu are real, and sustained upstream is what runs out first. "no cap" is not the same word as "unlimited", and the difference is the part that bites. custom rtmp every destination is a custom rtmp destination. there is no list of blessed platforms, because there is no integration tier to sell: a url and a key is all a destination has ever been. watermark none, anywhere. there is nothing on the page to advertise, and no plan above this one to advertise it to. your video stream-copied by default, so the picture that reaches each platform is the one your encoder made. optional shared renditions re-encode it, once, for the platforms that refuse your source. the trade the subscription does not disappear. it changes currency. self-hosting removes the per-channel tier, the watermark and the monthly invoice. it replaces them with five things, and you should price all five before you install anything. if any one of them reads as a dealbreaker, a hosted service is the correct answer and this page has done its job. a box, and its upstream one upload leaves your studio; the fan-out leaves the server. so the server needs roughly your bitrate multiplied by the number of destinations, in sustained upstream. cpu is rarely the wall, because video is stream-copied and only the audio is mixed and re-encoded; bandwidth is, and a domestic connection is usually the wrong place to put it. a domain and a certificate, if it leaves the lan the installer fits a self-signed certificate unless told otherwise, which browsers will complain about. let's encrypt needs a hostname that resolves and an email address, and the installer refuses to proceed without both. behind a proxy that already terminates tls, you turn it off here instead. an ffmpeg with the right things in it ffmpeg 8.0 or later, and it needs libsrt for the multitrack srt ingest that makes per-destination audio possible at all. homebrew's macos build ships without srt; ubuntu 26.04's carries it. the installer can fetch a pinned ffmpeg 8 build for you, and the container bundles one and sidesteps the question entirely. your own time, and your own pager there is no status page to refresh and no support queue to sit in. polyemesis ships prometheus metrics and alert rules with webhook delivery so that a stream which stops can page somebody, but the somebody is you, and at 3am nobody else is on call. that is the single honest difference between this and a subscription, and it is not a small one. linux, for anything you care about the broadcast path is tested on windows and macos in ci, and that suite has caught windows-only bugs before they shipped. what is not proven on windows is long-running service operation: the service wrapper is unexercised and recording can truncate on service stop. build and evaluate anywhere; operate on linux. why anyone accepts that trade one thing no plan on the list above sells. restream.io duplicates the single ingested stereo audio track identically across every enabled endpoint. read the plans above again for what the money buys: channels, a resolution, the removal of a watermark. none of them is an audio plan, so on any of them the mix that goes to twitch is the mix that goes to youtube. polyemesis takes the split audio tracks your encoder already sends (music on one, game on another, microphone on a third) and builds a different mix per destination from them, on the server, from one upload. the platform that mutes music gets the clean feed while the one that does not gets the full one, and neither costs you a second video encode. that is the whole reason to run a server rather than rent one. if you do not need it, the honest recommendation is to weigh the five costs above against a subscription and pick whichever you would rather pay. how the routing works → one install to a running server. docker, an installer script, or a single static binary. then point your encoder at it. install set up obs

h2: Three routes, and the cost each one moves somewhere else
Multistreaming from OBS to a server you run

/how-to-multistream-from-obs.text: guide how to multistream from obs to multistream is to broadcast one programme to several platforms at once: twitch and youtube and kick from a single run of the show. obs's stream tab takes one server and one stream key, so the second destination has to come from somewhere: a plugin running beside obs, a hosted service, or a server of your own. all three work. they fail in different places, and this guide is mostly about where. the three routes walkthrough what goes wrong pick one three routes, and the cost each one moves somewhere else the question underneath all three is where the copying happens: on the machine running obs, in somebody's cloud, or on a box you keep. every other difference follows from that one. details of the named products below were checked on 2026-08-15. route one a plugin, beside obs obs-multi-rtmp and aitum multistream both add destinations to obs itself. both are free, both are gpl-2.0, and both can either share the encode obs already made or run an independent re-encode per destination with its own resolution and bitrate. the cost is that your streaming pc does all of it. every destination is another upload leaving the house on the same connection that is already carrying the game, and every independent re-encode is another job for the card that is already encoding. obs-multi-rtmp is actively maintained; v0.7.4.3 was the current release on 2026-08-15. aitum ships this plugin at no cost. the separate aitum desktop suite, nexus, is $5.49/mo and is not required to run it. route two a hosted service restream.io takes one upload and replicates it from their cloud, so your uplink carries one stream no matter how many platforms are listed. nothing to install and nothing to operate. the cost is a subscription and a boundary. their free plan allows two simultaneous channels, to personal profiles and platforms, and excludes custom rtmp destinations along with facebook pages and groups, so a platform they have not integrated is not reachable on it at all. free-plan limits as published on 2026-08-15. plans move; the current page is the authority, and there is a fuller breakdown with dated prices on our free restream service page. route three a server you run obs sends one stream to a box you keep, and the box fans it out. datarhei restreamer is the long-standing option here: free, apache-2.0, self-hosted. polyemesis is the one this site is about, mit licensed, and exists for the audio difference below. the cost is that you now operate a server: bandwidth for the fan-out, an ffmpeg with the right options compiled in, and a pager that rings for you. it buys back the channel limits and gives the audio somewhere to be mixed. the walkthrough below takes this route, because it is the one with a step people reliably get wrong. on sending different audio to different platforms the plugins can do this, and it is worth being exact about how. they select a track obs has already mixed. building three different mixes therefore means configuring three track layouts in obs and encoding each output on the stream pc. polyemesis sums the tracks server-side, so one upload and one video encode feed every destination. restreamer is a different case: per egress target it can copy the audio, transcode the codec, or force silence, but it has no matrix for summing discrete channels into a new mix. restream.io duplicates the one ingested stereo track identically to every endpoint. walkthrough multistreaming from obs to a server you run six steps, about ten minutes. the one that catches nearly everybody is step four, and it is worth reading before you start: the multitrack path does not go through the stream tab. step 1 check that your ffmpeg speaks srt run ffmpeg -version and ffmpeg -protocols to confirm ffmpeg 8.0 or later with the srt protocol. without srt you are limited to single-track rtmp. docker bundles a known-good build and skips the check. step 2 run the server and set an admin password start polyemesis, open the ui on port 8080 and set an admin password. if it is lost, -reset-admin on the box sets a new one; there is no recovery from anywhere else. step 3 assign each obs source to audio tracks in the obs audio mixer, open advanced audio properties and tick which of the six tracks each source feeds. a typical layout is track 1 for everything, track 2 for the same mix without music, track 3 for the microphone alone. set a bitrate per track under settings, output, audio. step 4 configure the output in recording, not stream settings, output, output mode: advanced, then the recording tab. set type to custom output (ffmpeg), ffmpeg output type to output to url, container format to mpegts, paste the ingest url copied from sources, and tick the audio tracks to send. step 5 press start recording, not start streaming with ffmpeg output type set to output to url, the start recording button is the srt push. the ingest should appear live in polyemesis within a couple of seconds, with a meter per incoming track. step 6 add destinations and route the tracks add each platform as a destination, then tick which tracks it receives. play music and confirm on the meters that track 1 moves while track 2 stays flat before going live. the check in step one, in full: check ffmpeg copy ffmpeg -version | head -1 # 8.0 or later ffmpeg -protocols | tr ' ' '\n' | grep -x srt # must print: srt step four, field by field in settings → output , with output mode set to advanced, on the recording tab, with type set to "custom output (ffmpeg)". field value ffmpeg output type output to url file path or url the ingest url, copied from sources container format mpegts muxer settings leave blank video encoder libx264, h264_nvenc or h264_videotoolbox video encoder settings preset=veryfast tune=zerolatency video bitrate whatever you already stream at (it is copied, not re-encoded) keyframe interval (frames) 60, which is 2 s at 30 fps audio encoder aac audio bitrate 160 kbps audio track tick every track you want to send, up to 6 copy the ingest url out of the sources page rather than assembling it. it renders your own hostname and current settings, and it carries the token that tells the server which source you are. one port serves every source, and a publisher presenting an unrecognised token is refused rather than guessed at. once it works let obs press start for every destination the obs bridge starts the destinations you picked when obs starts streaming, and can stop them when it stops, with a grace period so a quick restart ends nothing. a scene change can apply a routing preset, so "just chatting" can drop the music track on one platform. it runs over obs-websocket, or from a script inside obs when polyemesis cannot reach your pc. obs bridge . if you would rather not depend on obs at all, turn on stop on ingest loss for the programme. if neither the primary nor the backup ingest arrives for the wait you set (two minutes by default), its live destinations stop instead of airing dead video. it watches the video arriving, so it works with any encoder, and it is off until you turn it on. what goes wrong four things that break a first attempt the stream tab looks like the right place and is not it can speak srt, and it sends one audio track, which loses the only reason to be doing any of this. multitrack srt lives under settings → output → advanced → recording, as custom output (ffmpeg) with ffmpeg output type set to output to url. that reads as wrong and is not: with output to url, the recording is the push. latency is written in microseconds 200000 means 200 ms, and it has to match the latency configured on the server's ingest. typing 200 gives you a fifth of a millisecond of buffer and a stream that comes apart on the first piece of jitter. an ffmpeg without srt, discovered late homebrew's macos build ships without it. ubuntu 22.04 (4.4) and debian 12 (5.1) ship an ffmpeg too old to start against at all. if the protocol check in step one prints nothing, use the container and stop debugging it. a "clean" track that is not clean play music and watch the meters before you go live: track 1 should move while track 2 stays flat. a clean feed that quietly carries the music bed is silent until somebody files a copyright claim, which is the worst possible moment to find out. one more, for completeness: obs 30.2 and newer can carry several audio tracks over enhanced rtmp, and every ffmpeg polyemesis supports demuxes it, but a run with obs itself as the publisher is still unconfirmed here. srt is the path that is operated and tested. use it. try it against a real box. docker, an installer script, or one static binary, then work back up this page from step two. install /twitch-vod-track.h1: The broadcast carries the music. The VOD track does not.
h2: What this page is not telling you
/twitch-vod-track.text: polyemesis / multistream / twitch vod track twitch the broadcast carries the music. the vod track does not. twitch can carry a second audio track alongside the live one, and use it for the vod. polyemesis builds that second mix from the same upload, so what your viewers hear live and what stays on the archive can differ, without a second encoder, a second upload, or a second stream key. before you install anything this is a twitch enhanced broadcasting capability, and twitch requires a gpu. a host that reports none is refused the negotiation outright, so on a headless vps, which is where a lot of self-hosted streaming lives, this particular feature will not come up. everything else polyemesis does works there; this one does not. it is also twitch-only. nothing in this project has measured youtube, kick, facebook or rumble accepting a second audio track, and the code declines to send one to them rather than guessing. one thing worth knowing if you came here from obs's own twitch vod track: that mechanism tags a second track with flv metadata, and obsproject/obs-studio issue #13636 (read 15 august 2026) reports it conflicting with enhanced broadcasting, with live audio archived regardless of the track exclusions. polyemesis does not use that path; it negotiates the second track through enhanced broadcasting itself. what twitch finally archives is still twitch's decision. what it actually does one ingest, one encode, one connection the live broadcast carries the music. the vod track does not. polyemesis builds both mixes from the tracks already arriving on your single srt ingest, and sends them to twitch over the same connection: your encoder uploads once and encodes video once. no video ladder required enhanced broadcasting is named for multitrack video, so the reasonable assumption is that you must send several video renditions to get a second audio track. you do not. requesting a single video track returns one rendition and both audio tracks, which is what makes this reachable at all for a server that copies video through untouched. a second mix cannot break your broadcast if the secondary mix will not compile, it is a warning and the stream goes out without it. an optional vod track must never veto a working broadcast. a primary mix that will not compile is still an error, because that one is the broadcast. adding it does not rewrite what you already send a destination that gains a vod track keeps its live mix byte-for-byte identical to what it produced before. turning the feature on is additive, and turning it off returns you exactly where you were. what this page is not telling you polyemesis builds a second mix and sends it. what twitch does with it, and whether any particular rights-holder agrees with the result, is not something this project can promise and nothing here should be read as legal advice. the mechanism is described above; the conclusion is yours to draw. the same mechanism has nothing to do with twitch in the general case. a second mix is only the two-destination version of what this server does everywhere: sum the tracks you choose, per destination, from one upload. the archive is simply the most common reason to want two. how the mix matrix works multistreaming, three ways install it

/calculator.h1: What a multistream actually costs your connection
/calculator.text: bandwidth what a multistream actually costs your connection two different connections carry two different loads. your encoder's upstream carries one stream. the server's uplink carries one per destination, but because polyemesis copies the video rather than re-encoding it, the video half is the same bitstream repeated, and it has to satisfy the strictest platform you send it to. simple verbose verbose adds per-destination bitrates, audio tracks, overhead and headroom. how often/much do you stream hours per stream streams per week destinations these are the bitrates each platform recommends , checked 2026-08-06. polyemesis ships the same figures as guidance and does not enforce them: nothing here refuses a value, and some platforms publish a higher maximum than the figure they recommend. youtube live 12000 kbps twitch 6000 kbps kick 1000-8000 kbps facebook live 4500-9000 kbps x (twitter) live 12000 kbps linkedin live 3500-6000 kbps rumble 4000-6000 kbps dailymotion 10000 kbps owncast 5000 kbps other rtmp or srt endpoints a company cdn, a second polyemesis, an nginx-rtmp box: anything with a url. name limit (kbps) add what you are sending video from your encoder (kbps) audio per destination (kbps) audio tracks from your encoder six is what obs sends. each one rides the ingest leg only. protocol overhead (%) rtmp framing plus tcp/ip. an estimate, not a measurement. headroom (%) a link run at its rated speed drops frames on the first burst. what you need encoder upstream (your home or studio) - server uplink (where polyemesis runs) - data moved from the server per stream - per week - per month - a month is 4.35 weeks. check it against your host's transfer allowance: that is the number a vps bills on, not the bitrate. how this is worked out encoder upstream = video + (audio × tracks). one stream leaves your encoder however many platforms you are sending to. that is the whole point of a restreamer. server uplink = the sum of what each destination actually sends. in simple mode every one takes the copied bitstream, so that is (video + audio) × destinations. give one a rendition and it sends its own video instead, and the sum stops being a multiplication. the recommendation that binds is the lowest among the destinations still taking the copied stream, because that is one bitstream they all share. a destination on a rendition is exempt: that is what the rendition bought. it binds your choice , not the software: nothing here or in polyemesis refuses a bitrate above it. renditions are shared, not per-destination. two destinations asking for the same bitrate cost one encode on the server and two uploads. a rendition re-encodes video only; audio is routed and encoded per destination either way. data = mbps × 450 mb per hour, times your hours. overhead and headroom are applied to the bandwidth figures; the data figures use overhead but not headroom, because headroom is capacity you provision and not bytes you send. platform figures are the bitrates each platform recommends, transcribed from the server's own preset table and checked 2026-08-06. they are advisory there too: polyemesis never refuses a value for being above one, and some platforms accept more than they recommend. protocol overhead is an estimate and varies with resolution, keyframe interval and network path.
